subject: Engineering Fundamentals
title: Satellite Orbits: GEO, LEO, and Everything Between
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Satellite Orbits: GEO, LEO, and Everything Between.

hook.text: A satellite in geostationary orbit stays over the same point on Earth. It orbits once every 24 hours — matching Earth's rotation.

buildup.text: GEO orbits sit at 35,786 km altitude. The distance adds signal delay — about 0.25 seconds each way — annoying for phone calls.

discovery.text: Low Earth orbit sits between 200 and 2,000 km. Satellites here move fast — orbiting every 90 minutes — but cover less ground.

twist.text: Sun-synchronous orbits pass any location at the same local time daily. Observation satellites use this for consistent lighting.

climax.text: Mega-constellations like Starlink use thousands of LEO satellites to blanket Earth in coverage with low latency.

punchline.text: Higher means steadier. Lower means faster. Each orbit serves a purpose.

quiz.question: Why is geostationary orbit specifically at 35,786 km altitude?
options: That altitude is above all atmospheric drag, keeping satellites stable indefinitely
At that altitude a satellite's orbital period matches Earth's 24-hour rotation
Geostationary orbit is the lowest altitude where solar panels receive full sunlight
